Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

issues.explanation: Relationship status 'Divorced' is implausible for age 21 under the validation rules.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: The profile lacks coherence with the trauma type and formulation because the dominant symptoms are generic hyperarousal/danger responses and self-harm, while there are no guilt, responsibility, shame, or perpetration-related appraisals/items that would typically anchor a profile for accidentally causing serious injury to another person. This makes the selected Threat and Memory content feel poorly tied to the identified trauma context.

issues.item: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
issues.explanation: Within the active formulation, Memory is strongly linked with Maladaptive Strategies and moderately bidirectional with Threat. The memory items support vivid, fragmented re-experiencing, but the selected maladaptive strategies do not clearly arise from managing those memories: Avoid Thinking fits, but Avoid People and especially Self-Harm are not well explained by the memory content provided.

issues.item: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
issues.explanation: Rage on Recall is the least coherent memory item for this trauma type in the absence of any corroborating interpersonal blame, anger-focused threat, or appraisals. For accidentally injuring another person, rage can occur, but standing alone alongside missing-memory fragments and sensory reliving, it is hard to integrate clinically compared with guilt, horror, or shame-linked recall.

The profile centers on a moral-injury-type accident in which the patient accidentally caused serious injury to another, but the dominant Memory item is intense rage on recall. Rage can occur, but in this trauma context it is much less coherent than guilt, shame, horror, or distress unless there is some clear target for anger, which is not reflected anywhere else in the profile.

Threat items are nonspecific hyperarousal symptoms (startle, sleep, concentration) that do not clearly connect to the selected Memory content or to a defined ongoing sense of danger. Given the formulation, Threat is mainly linked with Memory, so Threat items should plausibly arise from the memory content. Here the memory profile is fragmented, sensory, and rage-based, while Threat does not reflect a matching fear/danger theme, creating a weakly coherent Memory–Threat pairing.

vignette:
Mai sits in the chair across from me with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her knuckles pale against the worn fabric of her work jeans. She is thirty-eight years old, a welder, and she has not spoken to anyone about what happened in nearly four months. She tells me she is here because she cannot sleep anymore, and she is afraid that if she does not talk to someone, she will lose her job.

The event happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late September. Mai was working a double shift at the fabrication shop, finishing a rush order of steel beams for a construction site across town. She had been welding for fourteen years and prided herself on precision, on the clean lines of her beads, on never having caused an accident. That day, she was tired. She remembers that clearly—the way her eyes burned and her shoulders ached. She was tacking a support bracket onto a beam when a coworker, a man named Danny who had been at the shop for only three weeks, walked into her work zone without warning. Mai did not see him. She swung the torch to adjust her angle, and the arc caught him across the forearm. He screamed. The smell of burned fabric and skin filled her helmet. She remembers the taste of it—acrid, metallic, like copper and burnt hair—and she can still taste it now, sometimes, when she closes her eyes. Danny survived. He lost significant tissue and nerve function in his right arm. He has not returned to work. Mai has not spoken to him since the hospital.

What Mai remembers of the event is fragmented, incomplete. She remembers the scream, the smell, the taste. She remembers the foreman pulling her away. But she cannot remember dropping the torch, or what she said to the paramedics, or how she got home that night. The gaps in her memory terrify her. She has come to believe that the missing pieces mean she must have done something even worse than she remembers, that her mind is protecting her from the full truth of her negligence. She dwells on this constantly. She replays the moment over and over, searching for the split second where she should have looked, should have checked, should have known. She tells me she has gone over it a thousand times, and every time she arrives at the same conclusion: she should have been paying attention. She should have seen him. She is a professional, and she failed.

In the weeks that followed, Mai began to avoid people. At first it was small—she stopped eating lunch in the break room, ate alone in her truck. Then she started leaving the shop five minutes early to avoid walking past Danny’s empty station. Soon she was avoiding the grocery store, the gas station, any place where she might run into someone who knew. She stopped answering calls from her sister. She told herself it was easier this way, that she did not deserve company, that other people would only remind her of what she had done. The isolation felt like punishment, and punishment felt right.

At work, her concentration has deteriorated. She has made three errors in the past month—small mistakes, but dangerous ones for a welder. Her supervisor has noticed. She was pulled aside last week and told to take some time off. Mai is certain that if she loses this job, she will have nothing left. She is also certain that she deserves to lose it.

Sleep is a nightmare. She lies awake for hours, staring at the ceiling, her heart pounding, her mind cycling through the same loop of guilt and self-blame. When she does drift off, she wakes gasping, the taste of copper in her mouth, her body rigid with adrenaline. Strong physical reactions have become routine: the hiss of a welding torch, the smell of burnt metal, even the sound of a coworker’s footsteps approaching from behind—all of it sends her heart racing, her palms sweating, her chest tight with a terror she cannot name.

She has come to me because she is exhausted. She is afraid of what she might do if she keeps going this way. She is afraid of the dark thoughts that have started to surface, the ones where she wonders if Danny would be better off if she had never been born. She is not looking for forgiveness—she told me that flatly in our first session. She is looking for a way to stop the loop, to quiet the taste in her mouth, to be able to walk into the shop without her body screaming that she is a danger to everyone around her. She wants to work again. She wants to sleep. She wants to believe that she is not irredeemably broken. But she is not sure she can.
